newsitem.title: USA: Saudi bombing lapses held against U.S. general.
newsitem.headline: Saudi bombing lapses held against U.S. general.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen said on Thursday he was blocking the promotion of the Air Force general in charge of a housing complex in Saudi Arabia where 19 U.S. airmen were killed by a truck bomb last year.
The officer, Brig. Gen. Terryl Schwalier, now the Air Force's director of operations and training at the Pentagon, said he would resign.

Speaking after meeting President Bill Clinton on the matter, Cohen said he was singling out Schwalier for not doing enough to guard the barracks known as Khobar Towers from the June 25, 1996, blast in Dhahran.
"He's not being made a scapegoat. He's being held accountable," Cohen told a news briefing at the Pentagon.
Cohen faulted Schwalier, as the senior on-scene commander, for failing to adequately deal with the threat to the barracks' edge, only 80 feet (24 metres) from the nearest building.

"His chain of command kept him apprised of the level of the threat," Cohen said. But when Schwalier's subordinates failed to persuade Saudi officials to extend the fence-line even a small a small amount, he never raised the issue himself with his Saudi counterparts nor passed it up the U.S. chain of command, Cohen said.
Schwalier's failures "should not be imputed to all above him in the chain of command," the defence secretary said.
Siding with a Pentagon task force's original findings, Cohen overrode two Air Force reviews that found Schwalier had taken all prudent steps to defend his base.

But Sen. Arlen Specter, a Pennsylvania Republican who was chairman of the Intelligence Committee at the time of the blast, said Cohen's ruling did not extend accountability far enough. He said it should have gone straight up the chain of command to then-Secrertary of Defence William Perry.
In holding Schwalier responsible, Cohen cited the lack of an effective alarm system to warn of an impending attack and inadequate evacuation plans. Hundreds of troops were wounded.

The issue of whether to hold Schwalier accountable for Khobar security lapses deeply troubled the armed forces. Anticipating Cohen's decision, Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ronald Fogleman resigned on Monday, saying he felt "out of step" with Pentagon leadership.
At the time of the bombing Schwalier was commander of the U.S. air wing in Dhahran.

Schwalier had been approved by the Senate for promotion from brigadier general, a one-star rank, to major general, a two-star rank. The promotion was put on hold earlier this year, pending Cohen's decision.
The military's top uniformed officer, Army Gen. John Shalikashvili, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, endorsed Cohen's decision.
In what he called a message to young U.S. field commanders, Shalikashvili said the military must resist the temptation "to circle the wagons" for one of its own.
With his once-bright career prospects dimmed, Schwalier said in a statement that he had submitted his request for retirement, adding that he walked away with "head high."
